draft.title: Advertising to children
card: Children are easier to influence than adults. They may not tell an ad from other content, or see that its aim is to sell.
Ad Standards is the body that handles complaints about ads in Australia. Its codes set the rules for ads aimed at children.
The rules limit ads that could harm children, such as ads for unhealthy food and drinks. Ads must not pressure children or play on their trust.
Ads must also be clearly marked as ads, so a child can tell them from a show, a game or a video. This applies to ads in social media and online videos too.
draft.remember: Codes limit ads that could harm children, and ads must be clearly marked as ads.

a.q: Why are there extra codes for advertising aimed at children?
opts: Children may not see that an ad is trying to sell
Children never have any money to spend on products
Children do not watch television or use the internet
Children can only be sold healthy food and drinks
a.why: Children may not tell an ad from other content or see its selling aim, so extra rules protect them. Having little money is not the reason, as the rules are about how ads influence children.
a.clue: Think about how well a child can spot a selling message.

b.q: A popular video creator in Perth shows a new sweet drink in a video made for children. She was paid by the brand but does not say so. Which rule is most clearly broken?
opts: Ads must be clearly marked so children can tell they are ads
Ads for drinks may only be shown after school hours
Creators must not talk about any food or drink products
Ads aimed at children must always show the price
b.why: The video is an ad because the brand paid for it, but children cannot tell. The codes require ads to be clearly marked as ads. The rules limit some food ads but do not ban all talk of food and drink.
b.clue: Could a child tell this video is an ad?

a.best: Children may not see that an ad is trying to sell

b.best: Ads must be clearly marked so children can tell they are ads

problems.detail: The right option is the only hedged one ('may not'). Every distractor uses an absolute ('do not', 'never', 'only'), so a student can pick the answer by spotting the qualifier without knowing the idea.

check.summary: The card and both answers are accurate. In question a, the right option stands out as the only hedged choice among absolute distractors, so it can be guessed without knowing the idea.
